entries.23639d103583834bf5b8199e7b5e3fe15f6b1c2a: <div sID="gen11622" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="67" osisID="Ps.67" sID="Ps.67"/> <div eID="gen11622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11623" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11624" type="x-p"/> This psalm relates to the church and is calculated for the public. Here is, I. A prayer for the prosperity of the church of Israel, <reference osisRef="Ps.67.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. A prayer for the conversion of the Gentiles and the bringing of them into the church, <reference osisRef="Ps.67.2-Ps.67.5">ver. 2-5</reference>. III. A prospect of happy and glorious times when God shall do this, <reference osisRef="Ps.67.6-Ps.67.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. Thus was the psalmist carried out by the spirit of prophecy to foretel the glorious estate of the Christian church, in which Jews and Gentiles should unite in one flock, the beginning of which blessed work ought to be the matter of our joy and praise, and the completing of it of our prayer and hope, in singing this psalm.
entries.428ff3a89a3b888039dcb717cb0aef2495d8b8a7: <div eID="gen11624" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11623" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer for the Prosperity and Extension of the Church; Conversion of the Gentiles.</title> <div sID="gen11625" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> God be merciful unto us, and bless us; <hi type="italic">and</hi> cause his face to shine upon us; Selah. <hi type="super">2</hi> That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations. <hi type="super">3</hi> Let the people praise thee, O God; let all the people praise thee. <hi type="super">4</hi> O let the nations be glad and sing for joy: for thou shalt judge the people righteously, and govern the nations upon earth. Selah. <hi type="super">5</hi> Let the people praise thee, O God; let all the people praise thee. <hi type="super">6</hi> <hi type="italic">Then</hi> shall the earth yield her increase; <hi type="italic">and</hi> God, <hi type="italic">even</hi> our own God, shall bless us. <hi type="super">7</hi> God shall bless us; and all the ends of the earth shall fear him. <div eID="gen11625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11626" type="x-p"/> The composition of this psalm is such as denotes the penman's affections to have been very warm and lively, by which spirit of devotion he was elevated to receive the spirit of prophecy concerning the enlargement of God's kingdom. <div eID="gen11626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11627" type="x-p"/> I. He begins with a prayer for the welfare and prosperity of the church then in being, in the happiness of which he should share, and think himself happy, <reference osisRef="Ps.67.1">v. 1</reference>. Our Saviour, in teaching us to say, <hi type="italic">Our Father,</hi> has intimated that we ought to pray with and for others; so the psalmist here prays not, <hi type="italic">God be merciful to me, and bless me,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">us,</hi> and bless <hi type="italic">us;</hi> for we must make supplication for all saints, and be willing and glad to take our lot with them. We are here taught, 1. That all our happiness comes from God's mercy and takes rise in that; and therefore the first thing prayed for is, <hi type="italic">God be merciful to us,</hi> to us sinners, and pardon our sins (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.13">Luke xviii. 13</reference>), to us miserable sinners, and help us out of our miseries. 2. That it is conveyed by God's blessing, and secured in that: <hi type="italic">God bless us;</hi> that is, give us an interest in his promises, and confer upon us all the good contained in them. God's speaking well to us amounts to his doing well for us. <hi type="italic">God bless us</hi> is a comprehensive prayer; it is a pity such excellent words should ever be used slightly and carelessly, and as a byword. 3. That it is completed in the light of his countenance: <hi type="italic">God cause his face to shine upon us;</hi> that is, God by his grace qualify us for his favour and then give us the tokens of his favour. We need desire no more to make us happy than to have God's face shine upon us, to have God love us, and let us know that he loves us: <hi type="italic">To shine with us</hi> (so the margin reads it); <hi type="italic">with us</hi> doing our endeavour, and let it crown that endeavour with success. If we by faith walk with God, we may hope that his face will shine with us. <div eID="gen11627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11628" type="x-p"/> II. He passes from this to a prayer for the conversion of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">That thy way may be known upon earth.</hi> "Lord, I pray not only that thou wilt be merciful to us and bless us, but that thou wilt be merciful to all mankind, <hi type="italic">that thy way may be known upon earth.</hi>" Thus public-spirited must we be in our prayers. <hi type="italic">Father in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come.</hi> We shall have never the less of God's mercy, and blessing, and favour, for others coming in to share with us. Or it may be taken thus: "<hi type="italic">God be merciful to us Jews, and bless us, that</hi> thereby thy way may be known upon earth, that by the peculiar distinguishing tokens of thy favour to us others may be allured to come and join themselves to us, saying, <hi type="italic">We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Zech.8.23">Zech. viii. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen11628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11629" type="x-p"/> 1. These verses, which point at the conversion of the Gentiles, may be taken, (1.) As a prayer; and so it speaks the desire of the Old-Testament saints; so far were they from wishing to monopolize the privileges of the church that they desired nothing more than the throwing down of the enclosure and the laying open of the advantages. See then how the spirit of the Jews, in the days of Christ and his apostles, differed from the spirit of their fathers. The Israelites indeed that were of old desired that God's name might be known among the Gentiles; those counterfeit Jews were enraged at the preaching of the gospel to the Gentiles; nothing in Christianity exasperated them so much as that did. (2.) As a prophecy that it shall be as he here prays. Many scripture-prophecies and promises are wrapped up in prayers, to intimate that the answer of the church's prayer is as sure as the performance of God's promises. <div eID="gen11629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11630" type="x-p"/> 2. Three things are here prayed for, with reference to the Gentiles:— <div eID="gen11630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11631" type="x-p"/> (1.) That divine revelation might be sent among them, <reference osisRef="Ps.67.2">v. 2</reference>. Two things he desires might be know upon earth, even among all nations, and not to the nation of the Jews only:—[1.] God's way, the rule of duty: "Let them all know, as well as we do, <hi type="italic">what is good and what the Lord our God requires of them;</hi> let them be blessed and honoured with the same righteous statutes and judgments which are so much the praise of our nation and the envy of all its neighbours," <reference osisRef="Deut.4.8">Deut. iv. 8</reference>. [2.] His saving health, or his salvation. The former is wrapped up in his law, this in his gospel. If God make known his way to us, and we walk in it, he will show us his saving health, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">Ps. l. 23</reference>. Those that have themselves experimentally known the pleasantness of God's ways, and the comforts of his salvation, cannot but desire and pray that they may be known to others, even among all nations. All upon earth are bound to walk in God's way, all need his salvation, and there is in it enough for all; and therefore we should pray that both the one and the other may be made known to all. <div eID="gen11631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11632" type="x-p"/> (2.) That divine worship may be set up among them, as it will be where divine revelation is received and embraced (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let the people praise thee, O God!</hi> let them have matter for praise, let them have hearts for praise; yea, let not only some, but <hi type="italic">all the people, praise thee,</hi>" all nations in their national capacity, some of all nations. It is again repeated (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.5">v. 5</reference>) as that which the psalmist's heart was very much upon. Those that delight in praising God themselves cannot but desire that others also may be brought to praise him, that he may have the honour of it and they may have the benefit of it. It is a prayer, [1.] That the gospel might be preached to them, and then they would have cause enough to praise God, as for the day-spring after a long and dark night. <hi type="italic">Ortus est sol—The sun has risen.</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.8.8">Acts viii. 8</reference>. [2.] That they might be converted and brought into the church, and then they would have a disposition to praise God, the living and true God, and not the dumb and dunghill deities they had worshipped, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.4">Dan. v. 4</reference>. Then their hard thoughts of God would be silenced, and they would see him, in the gospel glass, to be love itself, and the proper object of praise. [3.] That they might be incorporated into solemn assemblies, and might praise God in a body, that they might all together praise him with one mind and one mouth. Thus a face of religion appears upon a land when God is publicly owned and the ordinances of religious worship are duly celebrated in religious assemblies. <div eID="gen11632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11633" type="x-p"/> (3.) That the divine government may be acknowledged and cheerfully submitted to (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">O let the nations be glad, and sing for joy!</hi> Holy joy, joy in God and in his name, is the heart and soul of thankful praise. That <hi type="italic">all the people</hi> may <hi type="italic">praise thee, let the nations be glad.</hi> Those that <hi type="italic">rejoice in the Lord always will in every thing give thanks.</hi> The joy he wishes to the nations is holy joy; for it is joy in God's dominion, joy that <hi type="italic">God has taken to himself his great power and has reigned,</hi> which the unconverted <hi type="italic">nations are angry at,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.11.17-Rev.11.18">Rev. xi. 17, 18</reference>. Let them be glad, [1.] That <hi type="italic">the kingdom is the Lord's</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.28">Ps. xxii. 28</reference>), that he, as an absolute sovereign, shall govern the nations upon earth, that by the kingdom of his providence he shall overrule the affairs of kingdoms according to the counsel of his will, though they neither know him nor own him, and that in due time he shall disciple all nations by the preaching of his gospel (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.19">Matt. xxviii. 19</reference>) and set up the kingdom of his grace among them upon the ruin of the devil's kingdom—that he shall make them a willing people in the day of his power, and even <hi type="italic">the kingdoms of this world shall become the kingdoms of the Lord and of his Christ.</hi> [2.] That <hi type="italic">every man's judgment proceeds from the Lord.</hi> "Let them be glad that <hi type="italic">thou shalt judge the people righteously,</hi> that thou shalt give a law and gospel which shall be a righteous rule of judgment, and shalt pass an unerring sentence, according to that rule, upon all the children of men, against which there will lie no exception." Let us all be glad that we are not to be one another's judges, but that he that judges us is the Lord, whose judgment we are sure is according to truth. <div eID="gen11633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11634" type="x-p"/> III. He concludes with a joyful prospect of all good when God shall do this, when the nations shall be converted and brought to praise God. <div eID="gen11634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11635" type="x-p"/> 1. The lower world shall smile upon them, and they shall have the fruits of that (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then shall the earth yield her increase.</hi> Not but that God gave rain from heaven and fruitful seasons to the nations when they <hi type="italic">sat in darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">Acts xiv. 17</reference>); but when they were converted the earth yielded its increase to God; the meat and the drink then became a <hi type="italic">meat-offering and a drink-offering to the Lord our God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.14">Joel ii. 14</reference>); and then it was fruitful to some good purpose. Then it yielded its increase more than before to the comfort of men, who through Christ acquired a covenant-title to the fruits of it and had a sanctified use of it. Note, The success of the gospel sometimes brings outward mercies along with it; righteousness exalts a nation. See <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Isa. iv. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.9">lxii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen11635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11636" type="x-p"/> 2. The upper world shall smile upon them, and they shall have the favours of that, which is much better: <hi type="italic">God, even our own God, shall bless us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.67.6">v. 6</reference>. And again (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">God shall bless us.</hi> Note, (1.) There are a people in the world that can, upon good grounds, call God their God. (2.) Believers have reason to glory in their relation to God and the interest they have in him. It is here spoken with an air of triumph. <hi type="italic">God, even our own God.</hi> (3.) Those who through grace call God their own may with a humble confidence expect a blessing from him. If he be our God, he will bless us with special blessings. (4.) The blessing of God, as ours in covenant, is that which sweetens all our creature-comforts to us, and makes them comforts indeed; then we receive the increase of the earth as a mercy indeed when with it God, even our own God, gives us his blessing. <div eID="gen11636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11637" type="x-p"/> 3. All the world shall hereby be brought to do like them: <hi type="italic">The ends of the earth shall fear him,</hi> that is, worship him, which is to be done with a godly fear. The blessings God bestows upon us call upon us not only to love him, but to fear him, to keep up high thoughts of him and to be afraid of offending him. When the gospel begins to spread it shall get ground more and more, till it reach to the ends of the earth. The leaven hidden in the meal shall diffuse itself, till the whole be leavened. And the many blessings which those will own themselves to have received that are brought into the church invite others to join themselves to them. It is good to cast in our lot with those that are the blessed of the Lord.  <chapter eID="Ps.67"/> <div eID="gen11637" type="x-p"/>

entries.0e325f68575999bdea2c25a70435a2d1583a8a66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6222"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 67</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.67.1-Ps.67.7">Psa 67:1-7</reference>. A prayer that, by God's blessing on His people, His salvation and praise may be extended over the earth.</title> <div sID="gen9515" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6222"/><hi type="bold">1. cause his face to shine--</hi>show us favor (<reference osisRef="Num.6.24">Nu 6:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.6.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.16">Psa 31:16</reference>). <div eID="gen9515" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2f403dbe774fa3b986c8c3ca54d6f4901623893: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6223"/><div sID="gen9516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6223"/><hi type="bold">2. thy way--</hi>of gracious dealing (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.8">Is 55:8</reference>), as explained by--<div eID="gen9516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saving health--</hi>or literally, "salvation." <div eID="gen9517" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d7fd1b6deeba8fa627e61564e4bd428cf717f4f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6224"/><div sID="gen9518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6224"/>3-5. Thanks will be rendered for the blessings of His wise and holy government (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Is 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4">11:4</reference>). <div eID="gen9518" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2d11dc407d7f6275be80041e1c3be4c26cf70e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6225"/><div sID="gen9519" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6225"/>6-7. The blessings of a fruitful harvest are mentioned as types of greater and spiritual blessings, under which all nations shall fear and love God. <chapter eID="Ps.67"/>

entries.c08cb5f2b957a7f3c48c70456b92c8fe7f4cd4eb: <div eID="gen20747" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20748" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20749" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20749" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20748" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20750" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prays for the enlargement of God's kingdom, <reference osisRef="Psa.67.1">Psa 67:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.67.2">Psa 67:2</reference>; calls upon all nations to serve him, because he judges and governs righteously, <reference osisRef="Psa.67.3-Psa.67.5">Psa 67:3-5</reference>; promises prosperity to the faithful and obedient, <reference osisRef="Psa.67.6">Psa 67:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.67.7">Psa 67:7</reference>. <div eID="gen20750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20751" type="x-p"/> The title here is the same with that of <reference osisRef="Psa.4.1-Psa.4.8">Psa 4:1-8</reference> (note), where see the notes. It is supposed to have been written at the return from the Babylonish captivity, and to foretell the conversion of the Gentiles to the Christian religion. The prayer for their salvation is very energetic. <div eID="gen20751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20752" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20753" type="x-p"/> God be merciful unto us - Show the Jewish people thy mercy, bless them in their bodies and souls and give a full evidence of thy approbation. This is nearly the same form of blessing as that used <reference osisRef="Num.6.25">Num 6:25</reference> (note), where see the notes.
entries.3573e2b2f23d0018dc0d94b0c9fae6ebf672294a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20754" type="x-p"/> That thy way may be known - That thy will, thy gracious designs towards the children of men, thy way of reconciling them to thyself, of justifying the ungodly, and sanctifying the unholy, may be known to all the nations upon the earth! God's way is God's religion; what he walks in before men; and in which men must walk before him. A man's religion is his way of worshipping God, and going to heaven. The whole Gospel is called this way, <reference osisRef="Act.19.9">Act 19:9</reference>. <div eID="gen20754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20755" type="x-p"/> Thy saving health - ישועתך yeshuathecha, "thy salvation." The great work which is performed in God's way, in destroying the power, pardoning the guilt, cleansing from the infection, of all sin; and filling the soul with holiness, with the mind that was in Christ. Let all nations - the whole Gentile world, know that way, and this salvation!
entries.84de652a6ad4d0232f3c43428e924910ced154b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20756" type="x-p"/> Let the people praise thee - When this is done, the people - the Gentiles, will praise thee; all will give thanks to God for his unspeakable gift.
entries.f8a567205532cc6fe7029376102b9fb346dc4ee1: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20757" type="x-p"/> Glad and sing for joy - They shall be made happy in thy salvation. Even their political state shall be greatly meliorated; for God will be acknowledged the supreme Judge; their laws shall be founded on his word; and the nations of the earth shall be governed according to judgment, justice, and equity. <div eID="gen20757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20758" type="x-p"/> Selah - This is true. There are innumerable facts to confirm it. All the nations who have received the Gospel of Christ have been benefited politically, as well as spiritually, by it.
entries.27b04d5380571a99ae3a2b82e0adf00a3ef756b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20759" type="x-p"/> Let the people praise thee - Seeing the abundance of the blessings which the Gentiles were to receive, he calls again and again upon them to magnify God for such mercies.
entries.80d659aa8d78216af54fc2a928c2fd2c4d649fa8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20760" type="x-p"/> The earth yield her increase - As the ground was cursed for the sin of man, and the curse was to be removed by Jesus Christ, the fertility of the ground should be influenced by the preaching of the Gospel; for as the people's minds would become enlightened by the truth, they would, in consequence, become capable of making the most beneficial discoveries in arts and sciences, and there should be an especial blessing on the toil of the pious husbandman. Whenever true religion prevails, every thing partakes of its beneficent influence.
entries.763e00ba4268cae7b583b1deb78a1ffdb0f847a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20761" type="x-p"/> God shall bless us - He shall ever be speaking good to us, and ever showering down good things upon us. <div eID="gen20761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20762" type="x-p"/> The last clause of the sixth verse should be joined to the seventh, as it is in several of the Versions, and should be in all. Many of the fathers, and several commentators, have thought that there is a reference to the Holy Trinity in the triple repetition of the word God: "God, our God, shall bless us; God shall bless us;" thus paraphrased in the old Psalter: "Blis us God the Fader: and our God the sone: and blis us and multipli us God the Hali Gast; that swa drede him God, all the endis of erth; for he wil comme to deme rightwysly that unrightwysly was demed. He that kan drede him, he eesses noght to lufe him." <div eID="gen20762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20763" type="x-p"/> When or by whom this Psalm was written cannot be ascertained. It seems to be simply a prophecy concerning the calling of the Gentiles, the preaching of the apostles, and the diffusion and influence of Christianity in the world. It is a fine piece of devotion; and it would be nearly impossible to read or repeat it with a cold and unaffected heart.  <chapter eID="Ps.67"/> <div eID="gen20763" type="x-p"/>

entries.16e88d1f9f1d68cc9cc1075a05c25826d4e1dd41: <div eID="gen9653" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Harvest Thanksgiving Song</title> <div sID="gen9654" type="x-p"/> Like <reference osisRef="Ps.65.1-Ps.65.13">Psa 65:1-13</reference>, this Psalm, inscribed <hi type="italic">To the Precentor, with accompaniment of stringed instruments, a song-Psalm </hi>(מזמור שׁיר), also celebrates the blessing upon the cultivation of the ground. As <reference osisRef="Ps.65.1-Ps.65.13">Psa 65:1-13</reference> contemplated the corn and fruits as still standing in the fields, so this Psalm contemplates, as it seems, the harvest as already gathered in, in the light of the redemptive history. Each plentiful harvest is to Israel a fulfilment of the promise given in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.4">Lev 26:4</reference>, and a pledge that God is with His people, and that its mission to the whole world (of peoples) shall not remain unaccomplished. This mission-tone referring to the end of God’s work here below is unfortunately lost in the church’s closing strain, “God be gracious and merciful unto us,” but it sounds all the more distinctly and sweetly in Luther’s hymn, “<hi type="italic">Es woll uns Gott genädig sein</hi>,” throughout. <div eID="gen9654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9655" type="x-p"/> There are seven stanzas: twice three two-line stanzas, having one of three lines in the middle, which forms the clasp or spangle of the septiad, a circumstance which is strikingly appropriate to the fact that this Psalm is called “the Old Testament Paternoster” in some of the old expositors.<note placement="foot">Vid., Sonntag’s <hi type="italic">Tituli Psalmorum</hi> (1687), where it is on this account laid out as the Rogate Psalm.</note> <div eID="gen9655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9656" type="x-p"/> The second half after the three-line stanza beings in <reference osisRef="Ps.67.6">Psa 67:6</reference> exactly as the first closed in Psa 67:4. יברכנוּ is repeated three times, in order that the whole may bear the impress of the blessing of the priest, which is threefold.
entries.4913d47c7ecd9fa4b7c118508155f95b72b5ad35: <reference osisRef="Ps.67.1-Ps.67.2">Psa 67:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9657" type="x-p"/> The Psalm begins (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.1">Psa 67:1</reference>) with words of the priest’s benediction in Num 6:24-26. By אתּנוּ the church desires for itself the unveiled presence of the light-diffusing loving countenance of its God. Here, after the echo of the holiest and most glorious benediction, the music strikes in. With <reference osisRef="Ps.67.2">Psa 67:2</reference> the <hi type="italic">Beracha</hi> passes over into a <hi type="italic">Tephilla</hi>. לדעת is conceived with the most general subject: that one may know, that may be known Thy way, etc. The more graciously God attests Himself to the church, the more widely and successfully does the knowledge of this God spread itself forth from the church over the whole earth. They then know His דּרך, i.e., the progressive realization of His counsel, and His ישׁוּעה, the salvation at which this counsel aims, the salvation not of Israel merely, but of all mankind.
entries.b12fce9b00809b5806c5aa5da4da4ec94d07d9c5: <reference osisRef="Ps.67.3-Ps.67.4">Psa 67:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen9657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9658" type="x-p"/> Now follows the prospect of the entrance of all peoples into the kingdom of God, who will then praise Him in common with Israel as their God also. His judging (שׁפט) in this instance is not meant as a judicial punishment, but as a righteous and mild government, just as in the christological parallels Psa 72:12., Isa 11:3. מישׁר in an ethical sense for מישׁרים, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa 11:4</reference>; Mal 2:6. הנחה as in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.4">Psa 31:4</reference> of gracious guidance (otherwise than in <reference osisRef="Job.12.23">Job 12:23</reference>).
entries.4dc3315424ee080498c7f70550bde9ec4c876fb6: <reference osisRef="Ps.67.5-Ps.67.7">Psa 67:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen9658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9659" type="x-p"/> The joyous prospect of the conversion of heathen, expressed in the same words as in <reference osisRef="Ps.67.5">Psa 67:5</reference>, here receives as its foundation a joyous event of the present time: the earth has just yielded its fruit (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.85.13">Psa 85:13</reference>), the fruit that had been sown and hoped for. This increase of corn and fruits is a blessing and an earnest of further blessing, by virtue of which (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.9">Jer 33:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.3">Isa 60:3</reference>; cf. on the contrary <reference osisRef="Joel.2.17">Joe 2:17</reference>) it shall come to pass that all peoples unto the uttermost bounds of the earth shall reverence the God of Israel. For it is the way of God, that all the good that He manifests towards Israel shall be for the well-being of mankind.  <chapter eID="Ps.67"/> <div eID="gen9659" type="x-p"/>

entries.4399f15e785694dec62b464d7a38862201e087f4:
PSALM 67
The following psalm contains a prayer for a blessing upon the Church, that besides being preserved in a state of safety in Judea, it might be enlarged to a new and unprecedented extent. It touches shortly upon the kingdom of God, which was to be erected in the world upon the coming of Christ.
With this agrees the opinion of the ancient Jews, who apply this psalm to future times, to the world to come, the times of the Messiah. The particular time and occasion of its composition can only be conjectured. Bishop Patrick thinks that it was probably composed by David, when, having brought the ark to Jerusalem and offered sacrifices, as promised in the psalm foregoing, verse 15, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord of Hosts, (2 Samuel 6:17, 18.) Horsley views it as “a hymn for the feast of tabernacles, prophetic of a general conversion of the world to the worship of God.” Calmet is of opinion that the composition of this, as well as of the two preceding psalms, was posterior to the return of the Jews from Babylon; and that the particular occasion was the restoration of fertility to the soil after the protracted drought and scarcity recorded by the prophet Haggai, (Haggai 1:10,11; 2:17-19.) But though the particular time and occasion on which it was written cannot with certainty be determined, it is evidently a prayer of the ancient Church for the appearance of the Messiah, and the universal diffusion of his gospel.
To the chief musician on Neginoth. A psalm or song.
Psalm 67:1-7
1. God be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us. Selah.
This verse contains a manifest allusion to the blessings which the priests were taught to pronounce upon the people of Israel, (Numbers 6:24-26.)
2. That they may know thy way upon the earth, thy salvation among all nations. 3. Let the people praise thee, O God! let all the people praise thee. 4. Let the nations be glad, and shout for joy; for he shall judge the people righteously, and thou shalt govern the nations upon earth. Selah. 5. Let the people praise thee, O God: let all the people praise thee. 6. The earth has given its increase; and God, even our own God!, will bless us. 7. God shall bless us,
God, even our own God, will bless us, God shall bless us. There is here again clearly an allusion to the formula of blessing in Numbers 6:24-26, where the name of God is, as here, repeated three times in succession.
and all ends of the earth shall fear him.
 
1 God be merciful unto us, and bless us The psalm contains a prediction of Christ’s kingdom, under which the whole world was to be adopted into a privileged relationship with God; but the Psalmist begins by praying for the Divine blessing, particularly upon the Jews. They were the first-born, (Exodus 4:22,) and the blessing was to terminate upon them first, and then go out to all the surrounding nations. I have used the imperative mood throughout the psalm, as other translators have done, although the future tense, which is that employed in the Hebrew, would suit sufficiently well, and the passage might be understood as encouraging the minds of the Lord’s people to trust in the continuance and increase of the Divine favor. The words, however, are generally construed in the form of a prayer, and I merely threw out this as a suggestion. Speaking, as the Psalmist does, of those who belonged to the Church of God, and not of those who were without, it is noticeable that yet he traces all the blessings they received to God’s free favor; and from this we may learn, that so long as we are here, we owe our happiness, our success, and prosperity, entirely to the same cause. This being the case, how shall any think to anticipate his goodness by merits of their own? The light of God’s countenance may refer either to the sense of his love shed abroad in our hearts, or to the actual manifestation of it without, as, on the other hand, his face may be said to be clouded, when he strikes terrors into our conscience on account of our sins, or withdraws the outward marks of his favor.
